title: Adolescence and Its Challenges
summary: Adolescence is the period of transition from childhood to adulthood, when the person changes physically and psychologically and new social roles are demanded; the child moves from dependency to autonomy. In the Indian social system it falls under Brahmacharya (apprenticeship), the first ashram. Erikson held that each life stage has a specific crisis; adolescents must integrate various roles into a consistent self-identity or they experience confusion over who they are.

Adolescence is a stage of stress, strain and storm with many ambiguities; uncertainty about one's role causes conflicts. Delinquency, suicides and drug and alcohol addiction may begin; career is planned and philosophies of life are moulded.

Adolescence is both. It begins with biological changes: the pre-adolescent growth spurt occurs in girls mostly at 9–12 years and in boys at 11–14 years, followed by secondary sexual characteristics: girls – rounding of hips, breast development, pubic hair, menstruation; boys – pubic hair, facial hair, change of voice. Its length is mainly social (when one leaves home, gets a job, can vote). Adolescents in western and eastern societies behave differently because of social norms, expectations and family structure.
## Factors determining the pattern of transition

Speed of transition (very fast change, little preparation); length of transition (early maturers are expected to act like adults; prolonged adolescence fosters dependence); discontinuities in training (trained to be dependent and submissive, now asked to take responsibility); degree of dependency (depends on childhood training; parents foster dependency); ambiguous status (in India the child follows parents' footsteps, in open societies each chooses own course); conflicting demands of parents, teachers, peers and community; degree of realism (looks like an adult but may not feel ready); motivation (insecurity lowers motivation; removing barriers raises it).

Developmental tasks are the problems individuals typically face at different periods of life. Havighurst listed ten for adolescents: new and more mature relations with age mates of both sexes; a masculine or feminine social role; accepting one's physique and using the body effectively; emotional independence of parents and other adults; assurance of economic independence; selecting and preparing for an occupation; preparing for marriage and family life; developing intellectual skills and concepts necessary for civic competence; desiring and achieving socially responsible behaviour; acquiring a set of values and an ethical system. Success brings success with later tasks; failure brings unhappiness and difficulty. In advanced cultures a person becomes an adult at the legal age; in simple cultures young people show adult status through puberty rites.

Pubescence is the beginning of adolescence. Growth spurt: girls about 10–11, boys 12–13 years, linked to the pituitary gland (controls adrenals, gonads, thyroid); rapid growth lasts 3–4 years, peak at average 12.6 years for girls and 14.8 for boys; a child may grow 6–8 inches and gain 18–22 kg in a year. Asynchronization: skeletal and muscular growth is faster than learning to use the new muscles; the lower face lags behind the upper; legs grow faster than the stem; hands and feet grow first. Sex hormones: testosterone in males, estrogen in females, secreted by the gonads. Sequence in girls: breast enlargement, pubic hair, menarche, axillary hair; in boys: testes enlargement, pubic hair, axillary hair, voice change, beard. Primary sex characteristics are the reproductive organs (menarche in girls, first ejaculation in boys); secondary are observable such as voice change and hair. Boys' strength rises with androgens, broader shoulders, bigger chest and lungs; girls' strength rises slowly because of biology and because culture encourages them to be weak and dependent. Average is not necessarily optimal.

Gender relates to a society's beliefs about traits and behaviours of males and females; gender roles are expectations about the roles and behaviour of each. Gender identity (knowing one is a boy or girl) is established by age 3–4; gender consistency (one remains the same sex despite changes in clothing or behaviour) is acquired at 6–7 years.

objective: The period of transition from childhood to adulthood marked by physical and psychological changes and new social roles.
Name any two secondary sexual characteristics of girls.
Rounding of hips, breast development, appearance of pubic hair, menstruation (any two).
Name any two secondary sexual characteristics of boys.
Pubic hair, facial hair and change of voice (any two).

Testosterone in males; estrogen in females.

objective4: Give the factors of the pattern of adolescent transition: (i) the pace; (ii) the duration; (iii) the training; (iv) the status.

vsa: Why is adolescence called a period of stress, strain and storm?
Rapid changes, ambiguity of role and conflicting demands bring conflicts, crises and dilemmas.
What is meant by asynchronization of development?
Skeletal and muscular growth is faster than learning to use the new muscle mass, so the body needs new learning.
Distinguish primary and secondary sex characteristics.
Primary are the reproductive organs (maturity shown by menarche or first ejaculation); secondary are observable features such as voice change and body hair.
What is meant by gender role?
Society's expectations of how males and females should behave and the roles they should perform.
How do advanced and simple cultures differ in giving adult status?
Advanced cultures give adult status at legal age; simple cultures require young people to show it through puberty rites.
Why are girls' strength levels lower than boys'?
Biologically boys have broader shoulders, bigger chests and better leverage; culturally girls are encouraged to be weak and dependent.
What is the identity crisis according to Erikson?
Failing to integrate various roles into a consistent self-identity causes confusion about who one is.
sa: Why is adolescence both biological and social?

It begins with biological changes of puberty and secondary sex characteristics, but its length depends on social factors such as leaving home, getting a job and voting; western and eastern adolescents differ owing to social norms.
Explain any three factors that determine the pattern of transition.

Speed of transition: very fast changes with little preparation; length: early maturers are expected to behave like adults, prolonged adolescence fosters dependency; discontinuities in training: trained to be submissive yet now asked to be responsible.
List the developmental tasks of adolescence (any six).

Mature relations with age mates; masculine or feminine role; accepting one's physique; emotional independence; economic independence; choosing an occupation; preparing for marriage; civic skills; responsible behaviour; values and ethics.
Describe the growth spurt in adolescence.

Girls at 10–11 and boys at 12–13 show rapid height and weight growth for 3–4 years, linked to the pituitary gland; peak at 12.6 years in girls and 14.8 in boys; a child may grow 6–8 inches and gain 18–22 kg in a year.
Explain the development of strength and skill in adolescent boys and girls.

Androgens, broader shoulders, bigger chest, lungs and heart give boys more strength, agility and coordination; girls' strength rises more slowly because of biological differences and cultural encouragement to be weak.
Distinguish gender identity and gender consistency.

Gender identity, known by age 3–4, is awareness of being a boy or girl though children are unsure it is permanent; gender consistency, by 6–7 years, is the understanding that sex stays the same despite clothes or behaviour.
la: Explain the physical development and sexual maturation in adolescence.

Pubescence brings a growth spurt controlled by the pituitary gland (girls 10–11, boys 12–13, peak 12.6 and 14.8 years). Asynchronization occurs as bones and muscles outgrow skills; proportions change. Sex hormones (testosterone, estrogen) cause primary and secondary sex characteristics in a fixed sequence; boys gain more strength.
Describe the developmental tasks of adolescence given by Havighurst.

He listed ten tasks: mature relations with age mates, gender role, accepting physique, emotional independence, economic independence, occupation, marriage and family life, civic competence, social responsibility, and a value system. Success leads to success later; failure leads to unhappiness. Cultures differ in giving adult status.
Discuss the major challenges and factors affecting the transition of adolescence.

Adolescence is a period of stress and storm with identity confusion. Factors: speed and length of transition, discontinuities in training, dependency, ambiguous status, conflicting demands, degree of realism and motivation. Delinquency, addiction and suicide may rise; removing barriers raises motivation.
What is adolescence? Discuss whether it is biological or social and the role of gender roles.

Adolescence is the transition from childhood to adulthood. Biologically it starts with puberty and secondary sex characteristics; socially its length depends on independence markers and cultural norms. Gender roles are society's expectations for males and females; gender identity develops by 3–4 years and consistency at 6–7.
